paper_title: A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement depends on both acquiring useful experience and recognizing when the current experience is no longer useful. Recent methods have emphasized what to generate next, such as harder problems or tasks near the models estimated competence. Yet system can continue spending updates on pool whose learning signal has declined, while refreshing too often consumes new tasks that may not be needed. This makes the timing of replacement distinct decision from the choice of replacement tasks. The answers attached to self-generated tasks raise separate reliability question. When training targets come from self-consistency or majority voting, errors in the models predictions can become labels for its next update. We therefore separate the source of refresh decision from the source of answer correctness: training dynamics can indicate when to draw new experience, while the new tasks should have independently checkable answers. We implement this separation in A-RSI (Adaptive Recursive Self-Improvement). In group-based reinforcement learning, prompts whose sampled responses receive different rewards provide nonzero relative-advantage signal. A-RSI monitors how many distinct prompts retain this signal, together with logged answer accuracy, and refreshes the active pool when the specified training-log condition fires. This is an operational indicator of declining learning signal, not proof that the pool has been mastered. The controller does not consult validation or test scores. fixed library of model-written programs supplies the new multimodal tasks. Each program constructs an image and question from sampled parameters and computes reference answer from the same underlying configuration. We specify this shared-configuration contract, machine-check selected reward and refresh properties, and independently audit generated answers. These checks support the use of program-computed supervision without asserting that every rendered question has been formally proved correct. The loop trains the Solver on the current pool, reads its training logs, and either retains the pool or activates prepared, unused replacement. refresh keeps the learned model weights; the task templates and sampling quotas remain fixed. The training stage uses no external training examples, human-written answer labels, or evaluation scores. In the tested Qwen comparisons, difficulty-aware and competence-aware replacement rules do not outperform random sampling under the fixed task-family shares. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, Qwen improves from 57.77 at the post-initialization checkpoint St to 61.05 after eight continuation windows and 800 fresh tasks. MiMo improves from 59.08 at its public base model S0 to 60.71. On the same eleven-benchmark protocol, A-RSI scores 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks, while every-window refresh scores 60.64 with 3,200. At the matched sixth continuation window, A-RSI scores 60.40 against 58.35 for continued training on the old pool. Figure 1 also motivates our response-level audit: score can rise because more answers finish within the output budget or because already completed answers are corrected. We report these outcomes separately. Our contributions are threefold: training-log refresh rule. We formulate pool-replacement rule using the decline in prompts with within-group reward variation, without consulting evaluation scores. Programmatically verified experience. Model-written programs instantiate multimodal tasks and compute their reference answers, allowing the training loop to operate without external training examples or human-written answer labels. Matched comparisons and output-level analysis. We compare refresh policies at matched training progress across full benchmarks and distinguish gains linked to response completion from corrections among completed answers. The Qwen results identify the benefit of the implemented replacement policy and the limits of the timing claim.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement research studies how system can produce useful experience and use it to improve. Prior work has changed the system around model, as in STOP and the Darwin Gödel Machine, or updated model weights from generated rationales, filtered samples, self-play, or model-based judgments (Chen et al., 2024, Singh et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2023, Yuan et al., 2024, Zelikman et al., 2022, 2024, Zhang et al., 2025). We focus on control question within weight-based improvement: how can system tell, without evaluation feedback, when its current training pool has stopped supplying useful signal? Our refresh decision comes from training logs; it does not adapt the task-generation rules during training. Table 1 compares how related systems obtain supervision and change their training data. Zero-data self-improvement and verifiable rewards. Absolute Zero uses an executor to validate codegenerated tasks and answers, while R-Zero trains Challenger and Solver to co-evolve around the Solvers current ability (Huang et al., 2026, Zhao et al., 2025). Multimodal work extends self-play through generated visual games or multi-role systems, including Vision-Zero and MM-Zero (Li et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026). These methods primarily develop how tasks are proposed, solved, or adapted. A-RSI instead fixes library of task-generating programs and studies when to draw fresh pool. Each sampled instance has programcomputed answer, so answer correctness does not depend on model vote. This distinction complements reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where methods such as GRPO and DeepSeek-R1 optimize against outcome checks rather than human-written reasoning traces (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025, Shao et al., 2024). DAPOs dynamic sampling also removes prompts whose sampled responses all receive the same outcome, since they yield no within-group policy gradient (Yu et al., 2025). We use the related signal for different decision: Uw aggregates informative prompts across window and helps determine whether the entire pool should be refreshed. It is pool-level diagnostic, not replacement for batch-level sampling. Procedural tasks and task selection. Programmatic generation provides an open-ended source of varied tasks, as demonstrated by Procgen for reinforcement-learning environments and by language-model resources such as Reasoning Gym and SynLogic for verifiable reasoning (Cobbe et al., 2019, Liu et al., 2025a, Stojanovski et al., 2025). Curriculum and adaptive-sampling methods address related but distinct problem: they prioritize examples or environments according to estimated difficulty or learning value. Examples include Prioritized Level Replay and PAIRED in reinforcement learning, and online difficulty filtering, bandit-based curricula, and distribution-level sampling for language-model training (Bae et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2025, Dennis et al., 2020, Jiang et al., 2020, Wang et al., 2025b). ThinkLite-VL is especially close to our setting: it uses search-based difficulty estimates to select smaller, challenging subset from fixed collection of visual reasoning examples (Wang et al., 2025a). Those studies motivate testing selection, but they do not settle how to choose replacement pool after training plateau. We compare difficulty-frontier, difficulty-ladder, and rollout-based selection with random draws under fixed family shares. In our experiments, the selection strategies do not outperform random replacement; this result is limited to our generators, model, and tested selection rules. Training duration and evaluation budgets. The apparent benefit of continued reasoning can depend on how generations are terminated and scored. Dr. GRPO analyzes response-length bias, DAPO includes overlong-reward shaping to address truncation, and L1 explicitly trains length-budget control (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025, Liu et al., 2025b, Yu et al., 2025). This work motivates separate audit in our setting: we check whether measured gain persists under longer generation budget and format-corrected scoring, including when evaluating released MM-Zero weights (Section 7.1). The audit is not new reward or refresh rule; it tests whether an apparent improvement reflects better task performance or only greater chance of completing within the evaluation limit. 5 Table 1 Comparison with related self-improvement and data-selection methods. Most change their training data continuously or at every step, whereas A-RSI replaces the whole pool only when its own training logs show saturation and refills it with random programmatic tasks. sections.content: Template construction takes place once, before training. Starting from seed task types in geometry, charts, tables, and counting, the base model generates reusable problem structures and writes their parameterized programs. For each structure, the model specifies the admissible parameters, the conditions and quantity to ask for, and the procedures for sampling values, drawing an image, composing question, and computing its answer. The resulting library stores these executable templates and stays fixed throughout training. The learner receives only (I, q), rather than the latent values or answer, and its response is scored against a. Replacement tasks require no further model call to generate their questions or reference answers. 6 Figure 2 Overview of A-RSI. Task templates, the candidate reservoir, and replacement pools are fixed before training. The controller reads training logs to decide when to activate fresh pool; only the Solver policy is optimized. Admission checks are specific to each generator: they test the sampled configuration, the answer computation, and applicable rendering and ambiguity constraints. Freshness and contamination screens then reject flagged candidates, and held-out diagnostic items are excluded from training. Retained records associate the image, question, and answer with generator identity and seed for reconstruction. These checks and independent answer audits are detailed in Appendix Q; program-computed supervision remains subject to the correctness of the template and its implementation. The generators build reservoir before continuation training. Candidates that pass the construction, freshness, and contamination checks and lie within the configured training ladders form the eligible set C, after excluding diagnostic holdouts. This set supplies the replacement pools. The initial pool comes from earlier geometry and chart batches with model-assisted question rewriting and checks. Generator allocations and reservoir sizes are given in Appendix Q.2.

Accordingly, Uw describes the logged training signal, rather than an exhaustive estimate of the pools remaining learnability. sections.title: 9 Discussion
sections.content: The simple version of the loop wins. The cheapest policy we found for keeping zero-data loop alive is to let the models training log say when the pool is spent and then supply random fresh tasks. Neither of the refinements we tried helped, and one made things worse. We read this as statement about this setting, in which the tasks are programmatic and the checkpoint is plateau. Measured state is for diagnosis. The ladder is useful for something other than selection. Because difficulty is measured, we can say what the model has learned, which tiers saturate first, and where mismatch occurs: for example, three of six ladders never reached the promotion threshold, and hard multihop tasks are largely length exhaustion. Self-assessed difficulty (AUC near 0.50) could not support these statements. Adaptation through observable training state. The controller connects experience reuse to the models ongoing optimization. MiMos changing decisions across pools and the divergent QwenMiMo final-round replay show why elapsed training alone does not specify the action. common fixed rule can respond to these differences through model-generated training feedback, without changing its thresholds or consulting evaluation performance. Limitations are discussed in Appendix U.

sections.title: P Evaluation Protocol and Noise Analysis
sections.content: Benchmark suites. The main suite contains nine benchmarks shared with earlier diagnostic evaluations: ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022), MMMU (Yue et al., 2024), MathVerse (Zhang et al., 2024), MathVision (Wang 39 et al., 2024), VisNumBench (Weng et al., 2025), MMSI (Yang et al., 2026), and the 4-option, 10-option, and vision versions of MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2025). The primary eleven-benchmark suite adds PhyX-MC and SCEMQA-MC, for 22,042 questions. The historical twelve-benchmark diagnostic suite instead adds MathVista (Lu et al., 2024), HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024), and MM-Vet (Yu et al., 2024), for 20,371 questions. Both use complete test splits. Macro11 and Macro12 are equal-weight means over their respective benchmarks, rather than pooled item accuracies. Evaluation schedule and metrics. Main trajectories, refresh-policy and selection ablations, endpoint audits, and the earlier-chain and extension benchmark comparisons use the eleven-benchmark suite and format-corrected scoring. The primary output limit is 8192 tokens; the per-window and earlier-chain tables additionally identify 4096-token results. Data efficiency divides the gain over St under the same suite, scoring rule, and limit by thousands of new training tasks. The fresh-pool completion decomposition uses all eleven benchmarks with the same equal-benchmark weights. The fixed 1,000-question sample and qualitative cases retain their stated item scopes. The length-budget comparisons use the same eleven-benchmark suite at matched output limits; earlier 16k and multi-hop diagnostics retain their explicitly stated historical scopes. Auxiliary views. Stable format keeps letter-, number-, and expression-gold items, applies format-corrected scoring to those same outputs, and equally averages the eleven benchmark subset accuracies (21,415 items). The sentinel is recomputed on the 114 yes/no items retained in the eleven-benchmark suite: COLLAPSE means accuracy below 70%; WATCH means accuracy below 74% or numeric-box share at least 10 points above the two-run St reference; otherwise it reports OK. Visual-type statistics use the original fixed labels restricted to retained benchmarks and exclude the unannotated science sets. Scoring and generation. Each evaluation samples one response per item at temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95. The prompt and original answer checker follow the public MM-Zero evaluation code (Li et al., 2026). The original matching procedure combines answer matching, unambiguous option-value matching, and MathVerify equivalence for non-letter gold answers. The format-corrected accuracy reported in the main and ablation tables retains those accepted answers and additionally accepts non-truncated unboxed final answers and normalized option values. ChartQA numeric answers receive 5% tolerance, except for year answers or questions asking for year. Truncation is recorded separately; length-limited response retains credit when the checker accepts its answer. Format checks reuse the same fixed responses, and each evaluation uses complete test splits at its stated output limit. LLM-judged accuracy. LJ uses Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with the MM-Zero judging prompt, answer extraction, and verdict parser. Questions of at most 400 characters retain their existing judge verdicts; longer questions are re-evaluated with the complete question. The judge receives the extracted final answer, falling back to the first 600 characters of the response when extraction is empty. Judging uses temperature 0 and 16-token output limit. Reported LJ scores equally average the eleven full benchmark sets. Measured variability on the eleven-benchmark protocol. Each policy arm was trained once. The four ladder-control runs with identical first-window data and seed score 54.74, 55.27, 54.45, 54.03 at 4096 tokens (range 1.25, sample sd 0.52). At window 2 and 8192 tokens, the ladder and truncation-aware runs, whose first two pool files hash identically, score 58.14 and 59.60 (difference 1.46). The two evaluations of the same St weights at 4096 score 54.55 and 54.72, differing by 0.17; their science outputs are shared, so this pair measures decoding variation only on the nine common benchmarks. These examples show variability but do not provide replicated uncertainty for each endpoint policy difference. Interpreting differences. We report descriptive single-run point estimates and stable-format checks. The available repeats do not estimate variation across seeds for each policy. Shared-prefix runs are not independent replications, and endpoint differences alone do not establish significance, equivalence, or superiority.

sections.title: Q Task Construction and Training Details
sections.content: Q.1 Template synthesis and task instantiation From seed types to templates. Given seed task types in geometry, charts, tables, and counting, the base model generates reusable problem structures and their executable implementations. For each structure, it determines the conditions and question target, chooses the variable parameters and their admissible ranges, and writes the procedures for sampling an instance, drawing it, composing its question, and computing its answer. These components form template τ . The resulting library is fixed before GRPO training. From templates to tasks. The seven generators in Table 30 select structures from the library and sample their parameters. Geometry parameters determine the points, relations, and given quantities. Chart and table parameters determine categories, labels, series, and numerical values. Counting parameters determine the objects and queried attributes. Each generator uses the sampled instance both to render the image and to construct the question and answer. For multiple-choice tasks, the program also constructs distractors and assigns the correct option its answer label. Execution and checks. Each candidate undergoes the checks implemented by its generator. Geometry checks compare the derived answer with the constructed relations or coordinate measurements. Chart checks compare the rendered marks with the underlying values and axis specification. Further checks reject ambiguous or invalid questions, and freshness and contamination screens decide whether an accepted candidate can enter the reservoir. Retained records include the image, question, answer, generator identity, and seed. Algorithm 2 summarizes the pipeline. Algorithm 2: Template synthesis and replacement-task construction Input: Base model, seed task types, generator allocation from Table 30 1 Generate template library with the base model; 2 Fix and initialize an empty candidate reservoir; 3 while generator has not filled its candidate quota do Select template τ and sample parameters pτ ; 4 Execute Gτ (z) to obtain image I, question q, and answer a; if construction, freshness, and contamination checks pass then 6 7 Retain (I, q, a) with its generator identity and seed; end 8 9 end 10 Exclude diagnostic holdouts and unsupported training cells to obtain C; 11 Draw disjoint 400-task pools from under the fixed family quotas; 12 Use the training-log detector to decide when to activate each pool; concrete geometry example. An initial-pool geometry template draws parallel lines AB and CD, with transversal meeting them at and H. The segment GM bisects BGH and meets CD at . The program samples the given angle β = BGH from 40, 42, . . . , 150 and constructs the point coordinates. When the question asks for the acute angle GM H, the answer is β/2. Sampling 64 therefore produces question with answer 32. The program recomputes the angle from the coordinates and rejects the instance if the two answers disagree. Q.2 Candidate reservoir and pool construction Candidate reservoir. We run the generators once before the continuation experiments to build the 16,000task reservoir in Table 30. After the construction checks in Appendix Q.1, candidates pass freshness check against earlier pools and task banks, an isomorphism-based contamination screen, and legacy contamination guard. We exclude 1,488 held-out diagnostic items and 30 plane-geometry items outside the configured difficulty ladders, leaving 14,482 eligible candidates. The two random replacement pools are prepared in advance and share no tasks. 41 Family mix and vocabulary. Each replacement pool contains 194 geometry, 131 chart, 54 table, and 21 counting tasks. The shares follow the visual-type counts of the 12 evaluation benchmarks: 4,912 geometry, 3,308 chart, 1,369 table, and 537 counting items (48.5%, 32.7%, 13.5%, 5.3%). Chart and table vocabulary also uses 19 thematic terms extracted from benchmark question text. These choices fix the task mix and vocabulary before training. The refresh detector does not read benchmark answers or scores. Function plots, numerical estimation, and spatial tasks are outside the current generator coverage. Table 30 The seven program-based generators and the candidate library. Gold answers were independently recomputed: mv 3,881/3,881, ref 1,568/1,568, tab/sc/ca 4,580/4,580, ga 150/150 on sample, and hr 1,922/1,927 (the five differences are ties for third highest, 0.03% of candidates). The initial 500 tasks come from three earlier generation batches, two for charts and one for geometry. The retained pool contains 204 geometry questions and 296 chart questions. Programs supply the answers, while the earlier pipeline uses an API-served Qwen3-VL-8B for question processing and checks. Of the retained questions, 342 use model-rewritten wording, 117 keep the original program wording, and 41 revert to it after rewriting. Pool selection uses eight-response probes and filters candidates by correctanswer count and truncation, with constraints on the question-type mix and reuse of each image. This pool is separate from the later 16,000-task reservoir. Two questions in the initial pool were later identified as configuration isomorphs of MathVerse items. Initialization and optimization. The starting checkpoint St follows 100 GRPO updates of Qwen3-VL8B-Instruct on the old pool. In the preceding plateau check, another 300 steps on the same pool changed the benchmark average by +0.45, 0.27, 0.38, and 0.63 across four training seeds. The continuation experiments start from St and retain that pool until their respective replacement rules act. The five-arm comparison reuses accepted checkpoints where the runs coincide. All arms except Continuous share the first two windows on the old pool, and A-RSI and Frontier also share the third. The first four windows of Continuous come from an earlier run of the same difficulty-control strategy, with fresh pools used from window 1. Training uses FSDP2 and colocated vLLM, with 100 optimizer updates per window and constant learning rate of 106. Each window starts with fresh optimizer and scheduler, retaining the preceding model parameters. Each prompt has eight rollouts, sampled at temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0 with 4,096-token response limit. generation batch contains eight prompt groups and serves two optimizer steps. The detector counts each batch once, giving 50 distinct batches and 3,200 responses per window. The GRPO objective uses group-normalized advantages, clipping threshold of 0.2, and no KL penalty. Dynamic resampling checks variance in correctness plus termination reward and excludes the format term, with at most six resampling rounds. The final optimization reward and logged advantages include all three terms. The detector reads those logged advantages after resampling. The reward coefficients in Eq. (2) are λfmt = 0.1 and λstop = 0.3, with unit weight on answer correctness. These coefficients stay fixed across windows. 42 The stopping term in Eq. (2) uses the decoders recorded finish reason and the final boxed answer. response that reaches the token limit receives 1 even if it contains boxed expression earlier in the text. Once response ends normally with final boxed answer, this term stays at 0 regardless of the response length. Its effect on truncation and benchmark scores is examined in Sections and 7.1. Refresh-controller settings. The controller in Eq. (4) uses lag ℓ = 2, minimum within-pool observation period nmin = 3, signal-retention threshold ρ = 0.85, and accuracy-increase threshold η = 0.10. The numerical tolerance in Eq. (3) is ε = 109. Thus, after at least three accepted windows on the same pool, decline of at least 15% in the distinct-prompt advantage signal or rise of at least ten percentage points in logged accuracy, relative to two windows earlier, triggers replacement. The initial pool contains 500 tasks, each replacement contains = 400, and each window has = 100 updates with = 8 responses per prompt. Replacement-family quotas are = (194, 131, 54, 21), as detailed in Appendix Q.2. All controller settings are fixed before training. Q.4 Diagnostic difficulty tiers For diagnosis we organize tasks into six controlled ladders: two multi-hop geometry ladders of five tiers, plane geometry of five, chart reading of ten cells, referring multi-hop of three, and counting of three. Each ladder orders related tasks from easy to hard. Accuracy is measured on held-out synthetic tasks that are excluded from training. Models own predictions of which questions they will get wrong give AUC about 0.50, program-based predictor 0.580.61, and measured accuracy of other models 0.720.82. At St, the pass rate falls monotonically with tier, for example .94, .57, .32, .14, and .07 from tier 1 to 5 on one multi-hop ladder. The comparison arms build frontier pools from these measurements (Section 6.2). For Frontier and Periodic, the frontier is the easiest tier in each ladder with held-out pass rate of at most 70%. If none qualifies, we select the hardest tier. The selected tier supplies 50% of the ladders quota, and each adjacent tier supplies 25%. Continuous re-measures pass rates after every window and moves the selected tier up one step at pass rate of at least 80%, down one step at pass rate of at most 20%, and otherwise keeps it unchanged. It uses the same allocation across the selected and adjacent tiers. These measurements do not affect random replacement or its refresh trigger.

sections.title: R Training Health Gate
sections.content: In the main Qwen experiment, window is accepted when its checkpoint export is complete, at least 50 generation batches are present, the learning rate remains 106 for all 100 updates, finish reasons are recorded, the training source has not changed, and the weights have moved. The weight check uses the median relative change of three sampled tensors, with threshold of 3.69 105. At least 97 of the 100 updates must have finite, nonzero gradient norms. failed window is retried once from the same preceding checkpoint with the same pool and seed. successful retry enters the detector normally. second failure halts the run. The trainer can also stop an attempt before all 100 updates complete: if six consecutive generation batches each contain at least one zero-advantage group after resampling, the attempt is aborted. This incomplete attempt fails the window gate and enters the same-pool retry procedure. The condition concerns the presence of zero-advantage group in each batch, even when other groups carry signal; it does not establish that every task in the pool has become uninformative. The detector, controller, probes, and pool builder use access guards that block benchmark scores and evaluation outputs. The legacy contamination guard runs separately and returns flag. An independent checker logged file accesses during the guarded processes and recorded zero test-set accesses. The earlier experiments required at least 99 of 100 updates to have normal gradients. Seven attempts failed at 98/100 across five windows. Fixed-pool continuation failed once at each of windows 10 and 11, and original-pool continuation failed once at window 3. Their retries passed, and the 8192-token comparison with MM-Zero uses the retrained fixed-pool continuation weights. Partial-pool refresh failed twice at window 12, and one ladder-control run failed twice at window 3. Both runs stopped. Each failure arose from single generation batch in which all eight groups had zero variance. The new experiments pre-registered threshold 43 of 97/100. In them, No-Refresh failed twice at window 7 with 94/100 normal steps, 35 zero-signal warnings, and training accuracy .728.

sections.title: S Engineering Notes
sections.content: File timestamps on the shared disk have one-second resolution and can lag. pre-registered ordering check based on modification times blocked arm No-Refresh at window 5 (two files written in the same second). The order is now proven by content hash chain, with modification times as coarse check with five seconds of tolerance, and the check is rehearsed with same-second mutants. The first version of the experiment was frozen and rebuilt as sagpd2 under the rule that each experiment is frozen only once. Quota exhaustion halted construction for about 11 hours once and left five machines idle; long dependency chains are now queued ahead of time. pre-registered health gate does block runs. Readouts are written as no reading and the gate is not relaxed afterwards. Command arguments must be quoted (an unquoted argument disabled depth feedback in one experiment), and base port plus stride times shard count must stay under 65,535. Zero-data discipline. Using the 70,000 public ThinkLite tasks as candidate pool was considered and dropped before any download, since it would violate the zero-data rule. Further Documented Issues in the MM-Zero Reproduction The following are observations in our reproduction setting and are not claims about the correctness of the released system. Reproduction. Published base and v5 scores reproduce (50.27 against 50.03, and 54.25 against 54.18). Local training reproduces three rounds (v1 +2.67, v2 +4.05, v3 +3.30 over base). Gain is mostly finishing, by four routes. Paired per-item analysis (4,006 base failures that did not finish, from 0.30 to 29.18); strict reproduction (7,257 finishing items, v1 +0.69, v2 +0.37, p-values above); an untrained base at 16384 matching MM-Zero at 4096 (51.12 against 51.08); and the pre-registered 8192 comparison (59% retained). Source and paper review. The two equations for the difficulty reward and the training label contradict each other; no image-necessity check (the figure-1 example can be answered without the image); text and table disagree (56.6% against 54.5%; the 4B block average differs from its cells by up to 0.89; 10 against 60 training steps; 5 against 8 rollouts; the same 8B base evaluated twice differs by 0.4 with no error bars); the central claim that three roles beat two has no experiment (the coder was never removed); one equation branch can never fire and another affects 0.03% of batches yet is credited with 2.9 points; labels have no program-based ground truth; the denominator drops truncated responses; about 16% of released images are almost entirely black. retracted accusation. We had earlier reported that MM-Zero lowers accuracy on items the base model already answers (1.28). With zero-effect baseline (the same model compared with itself gives 3.26) the change is +2.0 and there is no harm. That claim is withdrawn. Not done. 16k fair-budget comparison (about four node-hours), and mechanistic ablations of MM-Zero were not run.

sections.title: U Limitations
sections.content: Replication and evaluation horizon. Each arm was trained once. The main comparison spans eight continuation windows and has no 16k evaluation. Small score differences lack significance testing. NoRefresh halted at S31, leaving the pre-registered S32 endpoint unobserved. 44 Refresh timing. The first refresh point was set using existing logs. Without random-refresh control on fixed three-window schedule, the contribution of history-dependent timing remains entangled with the use of fresh tasks. Cross-model transfer. MiMo has positive fresh-versus-retained endpoint difference in one run, with small margins over Continuous and Periodic. Their pools were selected at Qwens difficulty frontier, limiting conclusions about transfer across model families. Generator scope. The fixed programmatic library covers geometry, charts, tables, and counting, but omits function plots, numerical estimation, and spatial tasks. Task-family shares and 19 thematic terms were informed by the evaluation benchmarks; diversity beyond these templates remains unmeasured. The initial task pool also contains model-rewritten questions with program-computed answers.
